questions.prompt: Compare `Array`, `Set`, and `Dictionary` in Swift. Explain when you should choose each one. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines Array as ordered with integer index and duplicate support
Defines Set as unordered unique items with fast membership checks
Defines Dictionary as key-value pairs with unique Hashable keys

questions.modelAnswer: An `Array` is an ordered list accessed by integer index, best when order matters or duplicates are allowed. A `Set` is an unordered group of unique items, best for removing duplicates and fast `O(1)` membership checks. A `Dictionary` stores key-value pairs with unique `Hashable` keys, best for looking up values by a key like a user ID.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Collection Types

questions.prompt: What happens when you read an out-of-bounds array index? How does this differ from reading a missing dictionary key? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that reading an out-of-bounds array index causes a fatal runtime crash
States that looking up a missing dictionary key returns nil safely
Explains that arrays use fixed numbered slots while dictionary keys can be missing

questions.modelAnswer: Reading an out-of-bounds index on an array causes a fatal crash at runtime because Swift expects an index to match a real numbered slot. Reading a missing key in a dictionary returns `nil` safely inside an optional. Keys are often missing in real apps, so dictionaries let you handle missing entries without crashing.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Collection Types

questions.prompt: Why must items stored in a `Set` or keys used in a `Dictionary` conform to the `Hashable` protocol? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Hashable creates an integer hash value used to find hash table buckets
States that hash tables give fast O(1) lookups
Mentions that Hashable builds on Equatable (==) so Swift can tell items apart if hash numbers match

questions.modelAnswer: Items in a `Set` or keys in a `Dictionary` must conform to `Hashable` so Swift can compute an integer hash value. Swift uses that hash value to find the hash table bucket, which gives fast `O(1)` lookups. `Hashable` also builds on `Equatable` (`==`), so Swift can tell two items apart if their hash values ever match.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Collection Types

questions.prompt: How does the default subscript `dict[key, default: value]` work, and why is it useful when counting items? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that it returns the saved value or the default value if the key is missing
Explains that it returns a non-optional value so you can update in place with += 1
Contrasts with manual optional unwrapping which takes extra lines of code

questions.modelAnswer: The default subscript returns the saved value for a key. If the key is missing, it returns the default value instead. Because the result is not optional, you can update counts in one line like `counts[word, default: 0] += 1`. This avoids extra lines of manual optional unwrapping.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Collection Types

questions.prompt: Explain how Copy-on-Write (COW) works for Swift collections and why it balances safety with speed. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: States that Swift collections are value types that share storage until changed
Explains that a new memory copy is only made when a write change happens
Notes that this avoids extra copying when passing collections to functions

questions.modelAnswer: Standard Swift collections are value types built as structs, so each variable keeps independent data. To avoid slow memory copies, Copy-on-Write shares the same storage buffer while copies are only read. When one copy changes, Swift makes a separate memory buffer for it. This keeps value safety without wasting time or memory on read-only passes.
